transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-04-29
- Time: 15:30 PDT
- Duration: 58 minutes (approx)
- Attendees: Maeve Carter (Redwood AE); Dev Patel (Redwood SE); Rita Sanchez (VeloxMed ML Lead); Tom Nguyen (SRE); Priya Rao (Product); Jake Miller (CTO)
- Recording: yes
- Shared artifacts: benchmarking deck + parity spreadsheet (link in notes); onprem-runbook.pdf (uploaded)

Auto summary (auto-generated, may be noisy): customer seeing "accuracy dip" after int8 deploy. possible root causes: quant noise, kv misalign, dequant math mismatch across kernels. request: run head-to-head on their prompts and provide rollback plan.

00:00:05 Maeve: ok hi everyone thanks for jumping on, quick intros, we got the notes from Rita and pulled a couple of perf traces. we'll go deep on the quant regressions and then map out bench tasks
00:00:22 Rita: thanks, yea hey um so short background — last month we flipped to a GPTQ-ish pipeline to drop cost for inference and we've started to see a drop on our clinical summarization quality for a subset of prompts, not across the board but it's visible in rouge-2 and a small set of user reports
00:00:38 Dev: when you say g-p-t-q pipeline, are you running per-layer gptq conversion or a fused awq style conversion? and which runtime are you using — the customer's runtime, or are you on the hosted redwood alpha?
00:00:52 Rita: it's an in-house conversion using bits-and-bytes fork earlier, so yeah per-layer gptq, we did a straight quantize and swapped model weights in our onprem cluster behind a VPC, we also enabled aggressive batching to amortize cost
00:01:08 Maeve: ok so two vectors — conversion variant (gptq vs awq vs int8) and runtime semantics, plus runtime settings like batching and kv cache. Tom, to confirm — you're on a private VPC deployment of the model?
00:01:19 Tom: correct, onprem with VPC peering to S3, we run Redwood Private early access. we also do sticky KV routing because sessions need continuity for long-chat summaries
00:01:30 Dev: sticky KV is key — if you have mismatch between how keys are cached (e.g., different dequant math ordering) you can see off-by-one drifts in generated tokens, that can cascade into rouge/bleu drop for summarization tasks
00:01:45 Priya: can you explain 'dequant math ordering' in simple terms?
00:01:48 Dev: yeah, so when weights are quantized per-layer, there are multiple steps to reconstruct floats — scale factors, zero points, and sometimes stochastic round. different libraries implement those steps in slightly different order or with different cast timings; small rounding differences early on can influence later tokens, especially in long prefix contexts
00:02:07 Rita: that kind of matches what we saw — the regression is more pronounced for longer clinical notes, runs fine for short prompts
00:02:14 Maeve: ok that's a good signal. it suggests a cumulative error/cascade rather than a single catastrophic mis-inference. two immediate test axes: 1) compare gptq vs awq and fp8 on same runtime, 2) isolate KV cache by running cold-starts vs sticky cache runs
00:02:35 Jake: we also saw mismatch between our local runner and a dry-run on redwood hosted earlier — numbers didn't line up, which made us suspect kernel-level differences
00:02:45 Dev: yep kernel selection and implementation differences (fused kernels, block sizes) will change rounding patterns. AWQ tries to preserve more head-level info in some layers which can help on summarization but may cost tokens/latency
00:03:00 Rita: so awq might help the quality but could blow our latency targets, we need <= 220ms p95 for 512 tokens ideally
00:03:10 Maeve: totally reasonable. to be explicit: we're going to measure both latency p50/p95/p99 and quality metrics (rouge, perplexity, a small human-annotated set) when we run the parity bench. we'll also collect kv hit/miss logs to see correlation
00:03:27 Tom: question: what do you mean by "kv hit/miss logs" and how invasive is that to enable on our onprem?
00:03:34 Dev: small change — we just record whether a token request hit the prefix cache vs went to compute, it's basically a counter and some per-session meta, low overhead. on VPC it just writes to S3 logs like we already do, nothing heavy
00:03:49 Priya: what about hybrid precision? like int4 only on some layers? we saw notes in your docs about layerwise sensitivity
00:03:57 Dev: good question. yes layerwise mixed precision — quantize most layers aggressively but keep sensitive ones in higher precision — is often best for quality/cost. we have tooling to generate per-layer sensitivity maps via a small metric sweep; that's part of the recommended workflow if head-to-head shows certain layers causing the bulk of degradation
00:04:14 Rita: do you have examples of layers that typically matter for summarization?
00:04:17 Dev: usually later decoder layers or certain attention heads that attend to long-range context. but it's model-specific — we'll run a quick per-layer ablation during the bench if you want but that costs time
00:04:29 Maeve: let's scope the bench first to the 5k prompt set Rita will share; if we see clear regressions we'll trigger layerwise sensitivity tests as follow-ups
00:04:39 Jake: latency impact — how much overhead does sticky KV add? we thought caching would help latency but it seems to sometimes increase p99 in your traces
00:04:48 Dev: caching helps amortize compute for repeated prefixes but introduces slight coordination overhead, especially with very high concurrent bursts and networked cache (VPC). we saw p99 blips when the cache node was getting saturated; smarter routing + local L1 sticky KV helps a lot
00:05:02 Tom: ok that matches our ops notes, we have a small window to add local L1 before shared cache but need config guidance
00:05:09 Maeve: we'll include a recommended KV topology with primary/secondary cache and backpressure thresholds in the runbook we share
00:05:18 Priya: what about FP8— is that a realistic compromise between INT8 cost and FP32 quality?
00:05:23 Dev: FP8 can hit a sweet spot: better dynamic range than INT8, often less layerwise sensitivity than GPTQ, and better fidelity on long-context sums. performance varies: on certain GPUs FP8 is faster than INT8 because of specialized kernels, on others not. so we need to test on your HW profile (which Tom will confirm)
00:05:41 Maeve: Tom, can you confirm the GPU/driver matrix and whether you have tensorcores supporting fp8 optimizations?
00:05:47 Tom: we're on A100s with driver x.y.z, planning a N2 upgrade later Q3 but for now A100s — we can also spin a small P4 cluster for smoke tests
00:05:58 Dev: A100 is fine; FP8 kernels are available in our private runtime but we need to match lib versions. I'll include exact build ids in the bench notes so you can reproduce locally
00:06:10 Rita: back to root cause, one of the oddities: when we turned off batching for a small subset, quality improved slightly. could that be due to different random seeds in batching codepath?
00:06:20 Dev: batching can change micro-timing and sometimes random seed ordering (e.g., dropout or sampling) — but for deterministic greedy/beam decoding it shouldn't. however quantized kernels sometimes use different numerics under batched execution vs single-call, so it's plausible
00:06:36 Maeve: we'll instrument the bench to run both batching=off and batching=auto with identical seeds and collect token-level diffs for a few failing cases
00:06:46 Priya: token-level diffs, that's expensive but useful — can you also provide a diff visualization?
00:06:51 Dev: yes we'll add a small diff tool output (which tokens diverged and when) and highlight first divergence position and subsequent cascading effect
00:07:03 Rita: timeline wise we need a patch path; if AWQ helps we might accept a small cost increase, but we need a rollback plan in case the canary shows worse user impact
00:07:13 Maeve: agreed — we'll propose a staged canary: start with synthetic canary tests on staging then a 1% traffic canary with auto-fallback to FP8 or FP32 on regression detection. we'll share the canary config and blast radius controls
00:07:28 Tom: what's the automatic regression detection signal — rouge drop threshold or some composite?
00:07:33 Dev: recommended composite: 1) Rouge-2 drop > 2.5% on canary set OR 2) Human-annotated failure rate increase > 1% OR 3) significant shift in perplexity quartiles. we can make thresholds adjustable but that's a safe starting point
00:07:50 Priya: any quick wins to try before the bench? like toggling layer 48 to full precision?
00:07:56 Dev: you can try warm-starting with mixed-precision on the top-k sensitive layers we suspect; but since we don't yet know which layers, it's somewhat trial-and-error. better to run the sensitivity sweep but we can trial a heuristic: keep last 4 decoder layers FP32 and quantize the rest — often helps for summarization tasks
00:08:13 Rita: that heuristic won't be too heavy on latency?
00:08:16 Dev: small p50 increase, p95 maybe nudges up depending on batch sizes. we'll measure it in bench
00:08:23 Maeve: ok process recap: 1) Rita provides prompt corpus and callouts 2) Dev runs parity bench (GPTQ vs AWQ vs FP8 vs FP32 baseline) with KV sticky on/off, batching configs, collects p50/p95/p99, rouge/perplexity, token diffs 3) we'll analyze and if needed do per-layer sensitivity 4) plan canary with rollback thresholds
00:08:45 Jake: curious — are there known implementations where gptq is actually better than awq in terms of preserving head-level attention? i've seen mixed notes online
00:08:54 Dev: historically GPTQ is very space-efficient and can be tuned for minimal MSE per-layer, but AWQ's algorithm tries to preserve attention matrices better at the cost of quant scale info; for some models AWQ beats GPTQ on downstream QA/summarization, for others the reverse is true — hence we need your data
00:09:12 Rita: can you briefly explain the 'dequant bias' term you used earlier? is that the same as 'quantization bias' people mention?
00:09:19 Dev: similar — dequant bias refers to systematic shift introduced when converting back from quantized values to floats (e.g., asymmetric quant scales or zero point shifts). if you have many such small biases across layers they accumulate. small bias in attention logits can shift sampling outcomes later
00:09:36 Priya: ok makes sense, we should also check initial weight distributions pre-quant to see if some heads already low-magnitude causing sensitivity
00:09:44 Dev: good point — we'll include pre/post weight histograms in the bench artifacts
00:09:49 Maeve: security/regulatory note — since some prompts are PHI-ish, please ensure data de-identification; Rita you'll confirm that the 5k set is de-identified before upload
00:09:58 Rita: yes we'll de-id and add a small test set with flagged sensitive prompts for manual review
00:10:05 Maeve: perfect. Tom any infra blockers for us running these parity tests on a staging cluster?
00:10:11 Tom: no blockers, we can carve out a small cluster for 48-72 hours for bench runs. need to schedule maintenance window for the peering config on Monday though
00:10:21 Maeve: we'll avoid that window. ok quick detour: Priya asked about canary traffic choreography — the rollback will be automatic tie-in to routing policy?
00:10:31 Dev: yes can be automatic: if rollback signal triggered we flip traffic using our routing layer to FP8/FP32 variant and then ramp down failing variant. we also log token diffs for forensics. we'll provide an example canary policy
00:10:44 Priya: are there any gotchas for SSO/audit when we flip models in VPC? audit trails intact?
00:10:50 Maeve: Redwood Private retains audit logs and we can push to your SIEM. we'll include the audit retention settings in the runbook
00:10:58 Rita: one more thing — our legal/compliance team asked if model artifacts or quantized weights ever leave our VPC during benching with Redwood — should be isolated
00:11:07 Maeve: for Private runs nothing leaves your VPC by default; when we run bench on your infra we only run code you approve and write logs to your S3 buckets. if we need to run hosted benches we will get explicit permission and use sanitized subsets
00:11:21 Dev: technical aside — to ensure bit-exactness we will version the quantizer (git/build id) and provide checksums for the quantized weight files so you can verify we used the same artifact as you locally
00:11:33 Jake: checksum step is good, we saw earlier mismatches due to older quantizer build on one node
00:11:39 Maeve: ok next steps and dates — we've covered those in action items. any last questions?
00:11:46 Rita: can you include an example of a rollback playbook in the docs? a runbook that non-ML folks can trigger?
00:11:52 Maeve: yes we'll add a playbook with step-by-step (who clicks what, signals to watch, how to force fallback) — aimed at ops people
00:12:01 Priya: and include a quick checklist for what to monitor during canary (rouge delta, latency, kv hit rate, token diff count)
00:12:08 Dev: noted — we'll produce a monitoring dashboard template and recommended alert thresholds
00:12:14 Maeve: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the links and schedule the bench.
00:12:20 Rita: thanks much

[Note: transcript continues with deeper technical Q/A and clarifying micro-issues; below are extracted segments from the longer discussion sampling the middle and end of the call to preserve fidelity]

00:23:12 Dev: (mid-call) on the subject of stochastic rounding — some AWQ variants use it to avoid large quantization jumps; stochastic rounding reduces bias on average but can increase variance which can look like instability in small test sets
00:23:31 Tom: is stochastic rounding deterministic across runs if you fix RNG seed?
00:23:36 Dev: depends on kernel and whether seed is exposed — some fused kernels don't expose seed control so you can't fully reproduce; that's a practical reproduction problem we call out in the bench
00:23:48 Rita: that could explain non-deterministic regressions we saw day-to-day

00:34:05 Dev: (later) we also need to consider dequantizing into higher precision temporaries for certain ops — e.g., do matmult in fp32 even if weights quantized, it reduces accumulation error; will cost cycles but sometimes drastically reduces quality gap
00:34:20 Priya: how do we decide which ops to do in higher precision? automatic heuristic?
00:34:24 Dev: we can profile by computing per-op sensitivity with a small calibration set; the profiler indicates ops where higher precision yields big quality lift relative to cost
00:34:35 Maeve: that's part of the advanced knobs we can recommend after the first parity run

00:47:10 Maeve: (wrap) ok to recap — Dev will run the parity bench; Rita will upload data; Maeve will publish docs and canary/runbook; follow-up 60m the week of 2026-05-11. thanks everyone
00:47:25 Jake: thanks all
00:47:29 Tom: thanks
00:47:31 Priya: bye
00:47:33 Rita: bye

End of meeting.
